'''Robert Miller Hazen''' (born November 1, 1948) is an American [[mineralogy|mineralogist]] and [[astrobiology|astrobiologist]]. He is a research scientist at [[Carnegie Institution of Washington|Carnegie Institution for Science]]'s Earth and Planets Laboratory and Clarence Robinson Professor of Earth Sciences Emeritus at [[George Mason University]], in the [[United States]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-03 |title=Robert Hazen |url=https://robinsonprofessors.gmu.edu/about/robert-hazen/ |access-date=2026-09-03 |website=George Mason University}}</ref> Hazen launched the [[Deep Carbon Observatory]] in 2009 and served as its Executive Director until 2019.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2026-08-20 |title=Dr. Robert Hazen |url=https://carnegiescience.edu/bio/dr-robert-hazen |access-date=2026-08-20 |website=Carnegie Science}}</ref>
{{TOC limit|2}}

==Early life==
Hazen was born in [[Rockville Centre]], New York, on November 1, 1948. His parents were Peggy Hazen (''née'' Dorothy Ellen Chapin; 1918–2002) and Dan Hazen (''né'' Daniel Francis Hazen, Jr.; 1918–2016).<ref>{{cite web|title=About the author|url=https://www.chapters.indigo.ca/en-ca/books/the-diamond-makers/9780521654746-item.html|website=The Diamond Makers|publisher=Indigo Books & Music, Inc.|access-date=12 September 2017|language=en|archive-date=14 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180814001727/https://www.chapters.indigo.ca/en-ca/books/the-diamond-makers/9780521654746-item.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Dan Francis Hazen Jr. |url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/latimes/obituary.aspx?n=dan-francis-hazen&pid=182591986&fhid=11399 |access-date=30 August 2018 |work=Obituaries |agency=Los Angeles Times |date=18 November 2016}}</ref> He spent his early childhood in [[Cleveland]], near a fossil quarry where he collected his first [[trilobite]] at the age of about 9.<ref name=Smithsonian>{{cite news|last1=Fields|first1=Helen|title=The Origins of Life|url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/the-origins-of-life-60437133/#YQd9TtV1k6LWpiKD.99|access-date=12 September 2017|work=Smithsonian Magazine|date=October 2010|language=en}}</ref>

The Hazen family moved to [[New Jersey]], where Robert's eight-grade teacher, Bill Welsh, observed Robert's interest in his collection of minerals. Hazen later recalled "He gave me a starter collection of 100 specimens, mineral field guides, and mimeographed directions to Paterson and Franklin, New Jersey."<ref name=RoeblingAcceptance/> Hazen also had an early interest in music, starting with the piano at age 5, the violin at 6 and the trumpet at age 9.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Toutant|first1=Pamela|title=Robert Hazen|journal=Applause at Strathmore|date=May 2011|page=17|url=https://hazen.carnegiescience.edu/sites/default/files/2011-Applause_0.pdf|access-date=10 September 2017}}</ref>

== Education ==
Hazen worked on his B.S. and S.M. (Master of Science) in Earth Science at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] 1971. He started with the intention of going into chemical engineering, but he was captivated by the enthusiasm of David Wones and converted to [[mineralogy]]. With Wones as advisor, he completed a masters thesis on [[cation]] substitution in [[trioctahedral mica]]s; his publication in ''[[American Mineralogist]]'' was his first to be highly cited.<ref name=RoeblingPresentation/><ref>{{harvnb|Hazen|Wones|1971}}</ref> He completed a Ph.D. in Mineralogy & Crystallography at [[Harvard University]] in 1975. His thesis, with Charles Burnham as advisor, involved learning how to use a 4-circle [[diffractometer]] to do high-pressure [[X-ray crystallography]] and applying it to [[olivine]]. This became a focus of his early career.<ref name=RoeblingPresentation/><ref>{{harvnb|Hazen|Burnham|1973}}</ref><ref name=RoeblingAcceptance/>

While a NATO Postdoctoral Fellow at [[Cambridge University]] in England, Hazen worked with [[Charles T. Prewitt|Charles Prewitt]] to determine empirical relations for the effect of temperature and pressure on interatomic distances in [[oxide]]s and [[silicate]]s.<ref name=RoeblingPresentation/><ref>{{harvnb|Hazen|Prewitt|1977}}</ref>

==Geophysical Laboratory==
In 1976, Hazen joined the Carnegie Institution's Geophysical Laboratory as a research associate.<ref name=cv/> After a brief stint measuring optical properties of lunar minerals with Peter Bell and [[Ho-Kwang Mao|David Mao]], he started to do X-ray crystallography with Larry Finger.<ref name=RoeblingPresentation/> He later recalled, "It was a match made in mineralogical heaven: Larry loved to write code, build machines, and analyze data; I loved to mount crystals, run the diffractometers, and write papers."<ref name=RoeblingAcceptance/> They collaborated for two decades and determined about a thousand crystal structures at variable pressures and temperatures, work summarized in their 1982 book ''Comparative Crystal Chemistry''.<ref name=RoeblingPresentation/><ref>{{harvnb|Hazen|Finger|1982}}</ref>

Much of the work that Hazen was doing could be classified as [[mineral physics]], a cross between [[geophysics]] and mineralogy. Although the field had pioneering contributions from the [[Nobel Prize]] winner [[Percy Bridgman]] and a student of his, [[Francis Birch (geophysicist)|Francis Birch]], in the early- to mid-20th century, it did not have a name until the 1960s, and in the 1970s some scientists were concerned that a more interdisciplinary approach was needed to understand the relationship between interatomic forces and mineral properties. Hazen and Prewitt co-convened the first mineral physics conference; it was held on October 17–19, 1977 at the Airlie House in [[Warrenton, Virginia]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Liebermann|first1=Robert Cooper|last2=Prewitt|first2=Charles T.|title=From Airlie House in 1977 to Granlibakken in 2012: 35 years of evolution of mineral physics|journal=Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors|date=March 2014|volume=228|pages=36–45|doi=10.1016/j.pepi.2013.06.002|bibcode=2014PEPI..228...36L}}</ref>

===High-temperature superconductors===
[[File:YBCO-xtal-unit-cell-3D-bs-17-atoms-labelled.png|thumb|upright=0.7|A model of a YBa<sub>2</sub>Cu<sub>3</sub>O<sub>7</sub> [[unit cell]].<ref>{{cite journal | journal = Acta Crystallogr. | volume = C46 | issue = 3 | year = 1990 | pages = 354–358 | doi = 10.1107/S0108270189006803 | title = Untwinned single crystals of the high-temperature superconductor YBa<sub>2</sub>Cu<sub>3</sub>O<sub>7-<math>\delta</math></sub> | author = K. Brodt, H. Fuess, E. F. Paulus, W. Assmus and J. Kowalewski | bibcode = 1990AcCrC..46..354B }}</ref>]]
Cooled to very low temperatures, some materials experience a sudden transition where [[electrical resistance]] drops to zero and any [[magnetic field]]s are expelled. This phenomenon is called [[superconductivity]]. Superconductors have a host of applications including powerful [[electromagnet]]s, fast [[digital circuits]] and [[SQUID|sensitive magnetometers]], but the very low temperatures needed make the applications more difficult and expensive.  Until the 1980s, no superconductors existed above {{convert|21|K|C}}. Then in 1986 two IBM researchers, [[Johannes Georg Bednorz|Georg Bednorz]] and [[Karl Alexander Müller|K. Alex Müller]], found a [[ceramic]] material with a critical temperature of {{convert|35|K|C}}. This set off a frenzied search for higher critical temperatures.<ref name=pjford>{{cite book|last1=Saunders|first1=P. J. Ford; G. A.|title=The rise of the superconductors|date=2005|publisher=CRC Press|location=Boca Raton, FL|isbn=978-0748407729}}</ref>

A group led by [[Chu Ching-wu|Paul Chu]] at the [[University of Houston]] explored some materials made of [[yttrium]], [[barium]], [[copper]] and [[oxygen]] (YCBO) and were the first to obtain a critical temperature above the boiling point of [[liquid nitrogen]]. The YCBO samples had a mixture of black and green minerals, and although the researchers knew the average composition, they did not know the compositions of the two phases. In February 1987, Chu turned to Mao and Hazen, because they could determine the composition of small mineral grains in rocks. It took Hazen and Finger a week to determine the compositions; the black phase, which turned out to be the superconductor, was YBa<sub>2</sub>Cu<sub>3</sub>O<sub>7−δ</sub>.<ref>{{cite book|first1=C. W. |last1=Chu |chapter=4.4 Cuprates – Superconductors with a T<sub>c</sub> up to 164 K|editor-last1=Rogalla|editor-first1=Horst|editor-last2=Kes|editor-first2=Peter H.|title=100 years of superconductivity|date=2012|publisher=CRC Press/Taylor & Francis Group|location=Boca Raton, FL|isbn=978-1439849484|pages=244–254}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Hazen |first=Robert M. |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/20339965 |title=The Breakthrough: The Race for the Superconductor |date=1989-08-13 |publisher=Ballantine Books |isbn=978-0-345-36145-5 |pages=90–97 |oclc=20339965}}</ref>

Hazen, Finger, and colleagues determined that the crystal structure of the superconducting phase was like that of [[perovskite]], an important mineral in [[Earth's mantle]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Anonymous|title=Superconductor resembles perovskite|journal=Eos, Transactions American Geophysical Union|date=1987|volume=68|issue=12|pages=161|doi=10.1029/EO068i012p00161-01|bibcode=1987EOSTr..68Q.161.}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Subsequently, Hazen's group identified twelve more high-temperature oxide superconductors, all with [[perovskite (structure)|perovskite structures]], and worked on [[organic superconductor]]s.<ref name=Career>{{cite web|last1=Hazen|first1=Robert|title=Career|url=http://hazen.carnegiescience.edu/cv/career|website=Carnegie Science|publisher=Geophysical Laboratory|access-date=27 September 2017}}</ref>

==Origins of life==
[[File:Riftia tube worm colony Galapagos 2011.jpg|thumb|Hydrothermal vents support a great variety of organisms, such as these [[Riftia pachyptila|giant tube worms]] near the [[Galápagos hotspot]], and may have been where life originated.]]
By the mid-1990s, Hazen felt that his research had reached a "respectable plateau" where the main principles of how crystals compress were known. The questions he was asking were increasingly narrow and the answers rarely surprising. So he changed research directions to study life's chemical origins.<ref>{{harvnb|Hazen|2005|pp=xvi–xvii}}</ref> This opportunity came when a colleague at [[George Mason University]], [[Harold J. Morowitz|Harold Morowitz]], realized that the temperature and pressure at a [[hydrothermal vent]] might change the properties of water, allowing chemical reactions that ordinarily require the help of an [[enzyme]]. Enlisting the help of [[Hatten Yoder]], a specialist in high pressure mineralogy, they tried subjecting [[pyruvate]] in water to high pressure, hoping for a simple reaction that would return [[oxaloacetate]]. Instead, an analysis by an organic geochemist, George Cody, found that they obtained tens of thousands of molecules.<ref>{{harvnb|Hazen|2005|pp=1–8}}</ref>

The publication of their results, which seemed to support the [[Abiogenesis#Deep sea vent hypothesis|deep sea vent hypothesis]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://astrobiology.nasa.gov/articles/2014/6/24/hydrothermal-vents-could-explain-chemical-precursors-to-life/ |title=Hydrothermal Vents Could Explain Chemical Precursors to Life |last=Schirber |first=Michael |date=24 June 2014 |website=NASA Astrobiology: Life in the Universe |publisher=NASA |access-date=2015-06-19 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129051724/http://astrobiology.nasa.gov/articles/2014/6/24/hydrothermal-vents-could-explain-chemical-precursors-to-life/ |archive-date=29 November 2014 }}</ref> met with criticism, especially from [[Stanley L. Miller|Stanley Miller]] and colleagues who believe that life emerged on the surface. Along with the general criticism that organic compounds would not survive long in hot, high pressure conditions, they pointed out several flaws in the experiment. In his book, ''Genesis'', Hazen acknowledges that Stanley Miller "was basically right" about the experiments, but argues that "the art of science isn't necessarily to avoid mistakes; rather, progress is often made by making mistakes as fast as possible, while avoiding making the same mistake twice."<ref>{{harvnb|Hazen|2005|pp=110–111}}</ref> In subsequent work, the group formed biomolecules from carbon dioxide and water and catalyzed the formation of amino acids using oxides and sulfides of [[transition metal]]s; and different transition elements catalyze different organic reactions.<ref name=Career/><ref name=RoeblingAcceptance/>

===Homochirality===
[[File:Zwitterion-Alanine.png|thumb|The mirror-image forms of alanine]]
Organic molecules often come in two mirror-image forms, often referred to as "right-handed" and "left-handed". This handedness is called [[chirality]]. For example, the [[amino acid]] [[alanine]] comes in a right-handed (D-alanine) and a left-handed (L-alanine) form. Living cells are very selective, choosing [[amino acid]]s only in the left-handed form and [[sugar]]s in the right-handed form.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=William H.|last2=Foote|first2=Christopher|last3=Iverson|first3=Brent|last4=Anslyn|first4=Eric|title=Organic chemistry|url=https://archive.org/details/organicchemistry00brow_261|url-access=limited|date=2009|publisher=Brooks/Cole Cengage Learning|location=Belmont, CA|isbn=978-0495388579|page=[https://archive.org/details/organicchemistry00brow_261/page/n1066 1038]|edition=5th}}</ref> However, most abiotic processes produce an equal amount of each. Somehow life must have developed this preference ([[homochirality]]); but while scientists have proposed several theories, they have no consensus on the mechanism.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Meierhenrich|first1=Uwe|author-link=Uwe Meierhenrich|title=Comets And Their Origin: The Tools To Decipher A Comet|date=2014|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-3527412792|pages=164–165}}</ref>

Hazen investigated the possibility that organic molecules might acquire a chiral asymmetry when grown on the faces of mineral crystals. Some, like [[quartz]], come in mirror-image forms; others, like [[calcite]], are symmetric about their centers but their faces come in pairs with opposite chirality.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Guijarro|first1=Albert|last2=Yus|first2=Miguel|title=The origin of chirality in the molecules of life : a revision from awareness to the current theories and perspectives of this unsolved problem|url=https://archive.org/details/originchiralitym00guij|url-access=limited|date=2008|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry|location=Cambridge, UK|isbn=978-0854041565|page=[https://archive.org/details/originchiralitym00guij/page/n137 130]}}</ref> With Tim Filley, an expert at organic chemical analysis, and Glenn Goodfriend, a geochemist, Hazen cleaned large [[calcite]] crystals and dipped them into [[aspartic acid]]. They found that each face of the crystal had a small preference for either left- or right-handed forms of aspartate. They proposed that a similar mechanism might work on other amino acids and sugars.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Meierhenrich|first1=Uwe|title=Amino acids and the asymmetry of life caught in the act of formation|date=2008|publisher=Springer|location=Berlin|isbn=978-3540768869|pages=76–78}}</ref> This work attracted a lot of interest from the pharmaceutical industry, which needs to produce some of their drugs with a pure chirality.<ref name=RoeblingPresentation/>

==Mineral evolution==
{{main|Mineral evolution}}
At a Christmas party in 2006, the biophysicist [[Harold J. Morowitz|Harold Morowitz]] asked Hazen whether there were clay minerals during the [[Archean]] Eon. Hazen could not recall a mineralogist ever having asked whether a given mineral existed in a given era,<ref name=Mann>{{cite news |last1=Mann |first1=Adam |title=What Mineral Evolution Tells Us About Life On Earth – And Beyond |url=https://medium.com/@adammann930/what-mineral-evolution-tells-us-about-life-on-earth-and-beyond-7d9be193ea30 |access-date=11 August 2018 |work=Medium |date=31 October 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Wei-Haas |first1=Maya |title=Life and Rocks May Have Co-Evolved on Earth |url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/life-and-rocks-may-have-co-evolved-on-earth-180957807/ |access-date=26 September 2017 |work=[[Smithsonian (magazine)|Smithsonian]] |language=en}}</ref> and it occurred to him that no one had ever explored how Earth's mineralogy changed over time. He worked on this question for a year with his closest colleague, geochemist [[Dimitri Sverjensky]] at [[Johns Hopkins University]], and some other collaborators including a mineralogist, Robert Downs; a [[petrology|petrologist]], John Ferry; and a [[geobiology|geobiologist]], Dominic Papineau. The result was a paper in ''American Mineralogist'' that provided a new historical context to mineralogy that they called [[mineral evolution]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hazen |first1=Robert |title=Mineral Evolution |url=https://hazen.carnegiescience.edu/research/mineral-evolution |website=Carnegie Science |access-date=12 August 2018 |language=en}}</ref>

Based on a review of the literature, Hazen and his co-authors estimated that the number of minerals in the [[Solar System]] has grown from about a dozen at the time of its formation to over 4300 at present. (As of 2026, the latter number has grown to 6239.<ref name="IMAMineralsCount">{{cite web | url=https://cnmnc.units.it/files/editor/IMA_Master_List_(2026-09).pdf | title=The New IMA List of Minerals – A Work in Progress | publisher=[[International Mineralogical Association|IMA]] – CNMNC (Commission on New Minerals Nomenclature and Classification) | website=The New IMA List of Minerals | date=September 2026 | access-date=3 September 2026 | author=Pasero, Marco | display-authors=etal | archive-date= | archive-url= }}</ref>). They predicted that there was a systematic increase in the number of mineral species over time, and identified three main eras of change: the formation of the Solar System and planets; the reworking of crust and mantle and the onset of [[plate tectonics]]; and the appearance of life. After the first era, there were 250 minerals; after the second, 1500. The remainder were made possible by the action of living organisms, particularly the addition of oxygen to the atmosphere.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rosing|first1=Minik T.|title=Earth science: On the evolution of minerals|journal=Nature|date=27 November 2008|volume=456|issue=7221|pages=456–458|doi=10.1038/456456a|pmid=19037307|bibcode=2008Natur.456..456R|s2cid=205042578}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Berardelli|first1=Phil|title=Earth's Minerals Evolved, Too|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/earths-minerals-evolved-too|access-date=9 September 2017|work=Science|publisher=AAAS|date=14 November 2008|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Vasconcelos|first1=C.|last2=McKenzie|first2=J. A.|title=The Descent of Minerals|journal=Science|date=9 January 2009|volume=323|issue=5911|pages=218–219|doi=10.1126/science.1168807|pmid=19131619|s2cid=206517566}}</ref><ref name=economist>{{cite news|title=How rocks evolve|url=https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2008/11/13/how-rocks-evolve|access-date=10 September 2017|newspaper=The Economist|date=13 November 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Yeager|first1=Ashley|title=Microbes drove Earth's mineral evolution|journal=Nature|date=14 November 2008|doi=10.1038/news.2008.1226}}</ref> This paper was followed over the next few years by several studies concentrating on one chemical element at a time and mapping out the first appearances of minerals involving each element.<ref name=Bradley>{{cite journal|last1=Bradley|first1=D. C.|title=Mineral evolution and Earth history|journal=American Mineralogist|date=23 December 2014|volume=100|issue=1|pages=4–5|doi=10.2138/am-2015-5101|bibcode=2015AmMin.100....4B|s2cid=140191182}}</ref>

A “system of mineralogy” is a classification scheme for all known kinds of minerals. In 2019, Hazen proposed an "evolutionary system of mineralogy," a classification scheme grounded in the concept of mineral evolution and based on the detailed properties of mineral specimens.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Hazen |first=Robert M. |date=2019-06-01 |title=An evolutionary system of mineralogy: Proposal for a classification of planetary materials based on natural kind clustering |journal=American Mineralogist |volume=104 |issue=6 |pages=810–816 |doi=10.2138/am-2019-6709ccbyncnd |issn=0003-004X|doi-access=free |bibcode=2019AmMin.104..810H }}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Hazen |first=Robert |title=Evolutionary System of Mineralogy |url=https://hazen.carnegiescience.edu/research/evolutionary-system-mineralogy |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20260613222840/https://hazen.carnegiescience.edu/research/evolutionary-system-mineralogy|archive-date= 13 June 2026|website=Carnegie Science}}</ref> The evolutionary system is intended to complement the official mineral classification system of the International Mineralogical Association (IMA) system, which is supervised by the IMA's Commission on New Minerals, Nomenclature and Classification.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Burke |first=E.A.J. |date=2006 |title=The end of CNMMN ad CCM—Long live the CNMNC! |url=https://cnmnc.units.it/files/V2n6_SocNews_Lr.pdf |journal=Elements |volume=2 |pages=388}}</ref> Under the IMA system, each mineral species is defined by its unique combination of major-element chemical composition and crystal structure. The evolutionary system instead groups minerals into "natural kinds" by looking at how they formed, along with their real-world chemistry, structure and physical traits.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> This can result in a single IMA species being divided into multiple kinds. For example, whereas the IMA defines all diamond as one species, the evolutionary system recognizes several kinds of diamond distinguished by origin, including stellar diamond (formed in the atmospheres of stars), mantle diamond (formed in the Earth's deep interior), and impact diamond (formed when an asteroid strikes a carbon-rich deposit). Conversely, the evolutionary system combines some compositionally similar IMA species into a single kind, such as the magnesium- and iron-rich members of the tourmaline group. The evolutionary system also includes a variety of non-crystalline materials not recognized as minerals by the IMA, such as obsidian, amber and coal. The evolutionary system is being published in 12 parts.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hazen |first1=Robert M. |last2=Morrison |first2=Shaunna M. |date=2020-05-01 |title=An evolutionary system of mineralogy. Part I: Stellar mineralogy (&gt;13 to 4.6 Ga) |journal=American Mineralogist |volume=105 |issue=5 |pages=627–651 |doi=10.2138/am-2020-7173 |issn=0003-004X |pmc=8051151 |pmid=33867541 |bibcode=2020AmMin.105..627H }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Morrison |first1=Shaunna M. |last2=Prabhu |first2=Anirudh |last3=Hazen |first3=Robert M. |date=2024-10-01 |title=An evolutionary system of mineralogy, Part VIII: The evolution of metamorphic minerals |url=https://doi.org/10.2138/am-2023-9004 |journal=American Mineralogist |volume=109 |issue=10 |pages=1760–1784 |doi=10.2138/am-2023-9004 |bibcode=2024AmMin.109.1760M |issn=0003-004X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Deep Carbon Observatory==
In 2008, the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] provided an initial grant to support a 10-year international program—the Deep Carbon Observatory—to study Earth’s carbon cycle from crust to core, with special emphasis on four scientific themes: deep life, reservoirs and fluxes, deep energy, and extreme physics and chemistry. The program, with Hazen as Principal Investigator and Executive Director, eventually enlisted 1300 scientists from 55 countries.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Deep Carbon Observatory |url=https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/items/2b3b8e68-b34a-49d8-b03c-4e00e5c39267 |title=Deep Carbon Observatory: A Decade of Discovery |publisher=Carbon Observatory Secretariat, Washington DC |year=2019 |doi=10.17863/CAM.44064 |access-date=2026-09-11 }}</ref>

Hazen and his colleagues started the [[Carbon Mineral Challenge]], a [[citizen science]] project dedicated to accelerating the discovery of "missing" carbon-bearing [[mineral]]s.<ref name="Wilson">{{cite news|last1=Wilson|first1=Elizabeth K.|title=Worldwide Hunt For Missing Carbon Minerals Begins |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/worldwide-hunt-begins-for-missing-carbon-minerals/|access-date=9 September 2017|work=Chemical and Engineering News|publisher=American Chemical Society|date=21 December 2015}}</ref> This effort eventually resulted in the discovery of 31 new carbon-bearing minerals.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Carbon Mineral Challenge: A look back at a four-year experiment in big data mineralogy {{!}} Carbon Mineral Challenge |url=https://mineralchallenge.net/the-carbon-mineral-challenge-a-look-back-at-a-four-year-experiment-in-big-data-mineralogy/ |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=mineralchallenge.net}}</ref>

==Time's Second Arrow==
In 2023, Robert Hazen, Michael L. Wong, and colleagues published a paper in the ''Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences'' suggesting a new law of increasing functional information.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wong |first1=Michael L. |last2=Cleland |first2=Carol E. |last3=Arend |first3=Daniel |last4=Bartlett |first4=Stuart |last5=Cleaves |first5=H. James |last6=Demarest |first6=Heather |last7=Prabhu |first7=Anirudh |last8=Lunine |first8=Jonathan I. |last9=Hazen |first9=Robert M. |date=2023-10-24 |title=On the roles of function and selection in evolving systems |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=120 |issue=43 |article-number=e2310223120 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2310223120 |doi-access=free |pmc=10614609 |pmid=37844243 |bibcode=2023PNAS..12010223W }}</ref> This concept was later expanded for general audiences in the 2026 popular science book Time’s Second Arrow: Evolution, Order, and a New Law of Nature.<ref name="Hazen1">{{Cite book |last1=Hazen |first1=Robert M. |title=Time's second arrow: evolution, order, and a new law of nature |last2=Wong |first2=Michael L. |date=2026 |publisher=W.W. Norton & Company |isbn=978-1-324-10548-0 |edition= |location=New York, NY}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Curmey |first=Andrew |date=2026-05-15 |title='Time's Second Arrow' Review: Life as a Drop in the Bucket |url=https://www.wsj.com/arts-culture/books/times-second-arrow-review-life-as-a-drop-in-the-bucket-2107af8e |access-date=2026-10-27 |work=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref>

According to Hazen and Wong, evolution—defined as an increase in the complexity and diversity of a system over time—applies to both living and non-living things. In order to evolve, systems must be composed of interacting components, such as cells, molecules, or atoms, for which natural processes exist to generate multiple configurations that are subjected to natural selection for functionality. Thus, only a fraction of these configurations will persist.<ref name="Hazen1" />

Hazen and Wong’s proposed law is underpinned, and can be quantified by, the conception of functional information, originated by Jack Szostak in 2003 to rigorously define the information content of biological systems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Szostak |first=Jack W. |date=2003-06-12 |title=Functional information: Molecular messages |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/423689a |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=423 |issue=6941 |pages=689 |doi=10.1038/423689a |pmid=12802312 |bibcode=2003Natur.423..689S |issn=0028-0836|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hazen |first1=Robert M. |last2=Griffin |first2=Patrick L. |last3=Carothers |first3=James M. |last4=Szostak |first4=Jack W. |date=2007-05-15 |title=Functional information and the emergence of biocomplexity |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=104 |issue=suppl_1 |pages=8574–8581 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0701744104 |doi-access=free |pmc=1876432 |pmid=17494745}}</ref>

Although the evolution of complexity in systems is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics, they cannot be derived from it. As such, Hazen and Wong proposed the introduction of a complementary new law. Like entropy, it is also an arrow of time, one that operates episodically and independently.<ref name="Hazen1" />

Hazen and Wong’s ideas, cited over 200 times in the first three years since their PNAS publication, have received both criticism and support. Their work has been applied to a wide variety of topics, including cancer research, microbiology, and large language models.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lynch |first=Michael |date=2025-06-10 |title=Complexity myths and the misappropriation of evolutionary theory |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=122 |issue=23 |article-number=e2425772122 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2425772122 |doi-access=free |pmc=12167962 |pmid=40408411 |bibcode=2025PNAS..12225772L }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thomas |first1=Frédéric |last2=DeGregori |first2=James |last3=Marusyk |first3=Andriy |last4=Dujon |first4=Antoine M |last5=Ujvari |first5=Beata |last6=Capp |first6=Jean-Pascal |last7=Gatenby |first7=Robert |last8=Nedelcu |first8=Aurora M |date=2024-01-01 |title=A new perspective on tumor progression: Evolution via selection for function |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/emph/eoae021 |journal=Evolution, Medicine, and Public Health |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=172–177 |doi=10.1093/emph/eoae021 |issn=2050-6201 |pmc=11448472 |pmid=39364294}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Nancy Collins |last2=Marín |first2=César |date=2025-01-01 |title=Functional team selection as a framework for local adaptation in plants and their belowground microbiomes |journal=The ISME Journal |volume=19 |issue=1 |article-number=wraf137 |doi=10.1093/ismejo/wraf137 |doi-access=free |issn=1751-7362 |pmc=12406698 |pmid=40600879}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Burden |first1=John |last2=Cebrian |first2=Manuel |last3=Hernandez-Orallo |first3=Jose |date=2025-11-05 |title=Conversational complexity for assessing risk in large language models |journal=EPJ Data Science |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=78 |doi=10.1140/epjds/s13688-025-00592-4 |doi-access=free |issn=2193-1127|arxiv=2409.01247 }}</ref>

==Teaching==
As the Clarence B. Robinson Professor at George Mason University, Hazen developed innovative courses to promote [[scientific literacy]] in both scientists and non-scientists.<ref name=DistinguishedPresentation/> With physicist [[James Trefil]], he developed a course that they described as "science appreciation", aimed at non-scientists. It was organized around a total of 20 "Great Ideas of Science" that were later reduced to 18.<ref name=Pool>{{cite journal|last1=Pool|first1=R.|title=Science Literacy: The Enemy Is Us|journal=Science|date=18 January 1991|volume=251|issue=4991|pages=266–267|doi=10.1126/science.251.4991.266|pmid=17733275|bibcode=1991Sci...251..266P}}</ref><ref name=freshman>{{cite journal|last1=Pool|first1=R.|title=Freshman Chemistry Was Never Like This: To battle science illiteracy among college students, the New Liberal Arts program tries a fresh approach to teaching science|journal=Science|date=13 April 1990|volume=248|issue=4952|pages=157–158|doi=10.1126/science.248.4952.157|pmid=17740124|bibcode=1990Sci...248..157P}}</ref> In addition to writing about their ideas in several magazines, they turned the course into a book, ''Science Matters: Achieving Scientific Literacy.'' They used the principles to organize explanations of a "vast number of socially significant, fundamental, or environmentally crucial topics."<ref name=Kauffman>{{cite journal|last1=Kauffman|first1=George B.|title=Science matters: Achieving scientific literacy (Hazen, Robert M.; Trefil, James)|journal=Journal of Chemical Education|date=August 1991|volume=68|issue=8|page=A213|doi=10.1021/ed068pA213|bibcode=1991JChEd..68..213K|doi-access=}}</ref> This was published with an amount of advance publicity that was unusual for a popular science book, including an article they wrote for the ''[[New York Times Sunday Magazine]]'',<ref name=quark>{{cite news|last1=Hazen|first1=Robert M.|last2=Trefil|first2=James|author-link=James Trefil|title=Quick! What's a quark?|work=The New York Times Magazine|date=13 January 1991}}</ref> praise from prolific author [[Isaac Asimov]] and physics Nobelist [[Leon Lederman]], and a publicity tour.<ref name=Kauffman/> For an article in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' about the book, they provided the author with the original list of 20 ideas and invited readers to send in their comments.<ref name=Pool/> About 200 readers responded, generally supporting the idea of such a list while vehemently criticizing many of the particulars, including an informal style and sometimes vague language. Particularly criticized were numbers 1 ("The universe is regular and predictable") and 16 ("Everything on the earth operates in cycles").<ref name=lumps>{{cite journal|last1=Culotta|first1=Elizabeth|title=Science's 20 Greatest Hits Take Their Lumps|journal=Science|date=15 March 1991|volume=251|issue=4999|pages=1308–1309|doi=10.1126/science.251.4999.1308|pmid=17816173|bibcode=1991Sci...251.1308C}}</ref> Hazen and Trefil argued, in defense of point 1, that it was not intended as a defense of determinism and that they covered unpredictable phenomena like [[chaos theory|chaos]];<ref name=lumps/> but they also used the responses to modify the list of ideas in subsequent editions.

Hazen and Trefil went on to write three undergraduate textbooks: ''The Sciences: An Integrated Approach'' (1993),<ref>{{cite book|last1=Trefil|first1=James|author-link1=James Trefil|last2=Hazen|first2=Robert M.|title=The sciences : an integrated approach|date=1994|publisher=Wiley|location=New York|isbn=978-0471303008|edition=A preliminary}}</ref> ''The Physical Sciences: An Integrated Approach'' (1995),<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hazen|first1=Robert M.|last2=Trefil|first2=James|author-link2=James Trefil|title=The Physical sciences : an integrated approach|date=1996|publisher=Wiley|location=New York|isbn=978-0471002499}}</ref> and ''Physics Matters: An Introduction to Conceptual Physics'' (2004).<ref>{{cite book|last1=Trefil|first1=James|author-link=James Trefil|last2=Hazen|first2=Robert M.|title=Physics matter : an introduction to conceptual physics|date=2004|publisher=J. Wiley|isbn=978-0471150589}}</ref> Hazen used these as the basis for a 60-lecture video and audio course called ''[[The Joy of Science]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Robert Hazen|url=https://robinsonprofessors.gmu.edu/about/robert-hazen/|website=Robinson Professors|publisher=George Mason University|access-date=13 May 2018|date=8 October 2010}}</ref><ref name=DistinguishedPresentation/>

==Public engagement==
In 2008, Hazen was an outgoing member of the AAAS Committee on Public Understanding of Science and Technology. He and his wife Margee, noting that it is important for scientists to engage with the public but actually doing so does not help them get tenure, proposed a new award, The Early Career Award for Public Engagement with Science, and established a fund for it.<ref>{{cite web|title=Special gifts and projects 2009|url=https://www.aaas.org/sites/default/files/AnnualReports/2009/aaas_ann_rpt_09j_gifts_projects.pdf|website=2009 Annual Report|publisher=AAAS|access-date=10 September 2017}}</ref> The first award, with a monetary prize of $5,000, was announced in 2010.<ref>{{cite web|title=Early Career Award for Public Engagement with Science Recipients|url=https://www.aaas.org/page/early-career-award-public-engagement-science-recipients|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science|access-date=10 September 2017|language=en|date=27 June 2013}}</ref>

==Honors==
Hazen is a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].

The [[Mineralogical Society of America]] presented Hazen with the Mineralogical Society of America Award in 1982 and the Distinguished Public Service Medal in 2009.<ref name=DistinguishedPresentation>{{cite journal|last1=Hemley|first1=R. J.|title=Presentation of the Distinguished Public Service Medal of the Mineralogical Society of America for 2009|journal=American Mineralogist|date=25 March 2010|volume=95|issue=4|pages=666|doi=10.2138/am.2010.557|bibcode=2010AmMin..95..666H|s2cid=96565994}}</ref><ref name=DistinguishedAcceptance>{{cite journal|last1=Hazen|first1=R. M.|title=Acceptance of the Mineralogical Society of America Distinguished Public Service Medal for 2009|journal=American Mineralogist|date=25 March 2010|volume=95|issue=4|pages=667|doi=10.2138/am.2010.556|bibcode=2010AmMin..95..667H|s2cid=97885867}}</ref> In 2016, he received its highest award, the [[Roebling Medal]].<ref name=RoeblingPresentation>{{cite journal|last1=Hemley|first1=Russell J.|title=Presentation of the 2016 Roebling Medal of the Mineralogical Society of America to Robert M. Hazen|issue=5|journal=American Mineralogist|volume=102|pages=1133|language=en|doi=10.2138/am-2017-AP10251|date=1 May 2017|doi-access=free |bibcode=2017AmMin.102.1133H }}</ref><ref name=RoeblingAcceptance>{{cite journal|last1=Hazen|first1=Robert M.|title=Acceptance of the 2016 Roebling Medal of the Mineralogical Society of America|url=http://ammin.geoscienceworld.org/content/102/5/1134|journal=American Mineralogist|access-date=9 September 2017|pages=1134–1135|language=en|doi=10.2138/am-2017-AP10252|date=1 May 2017|volume=102|issue=5|doi-access=free |bibcode=2017AmMin.102.1134H }}</ref> He also served as Distinguished Lecturer and is a Past President of the Society. A mineral that was discovered in [[Mono Lake]] was named [[hazenite]] in his honor by Hexiong Yang, a former student of his.<ref name=economist/>

In 1986, Hazen received the [[Vladimir Ipatieff#Ipatieff Prize|Ipatieff Prize]], which the [[American Chemical Society]] awards in recognition of "outstanding chemical experimental work in the field of catalysis or high pressure".<ref>{{cite web|title=Ipatieff Prize|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/ipatieff-prize.html|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=9 September 2017|language=en}}</ref>

For the book ''The Music Men'', he and his wife Margaret received the [[Deems Taylor#Deems Taylor Award|Deems Taylor Award]] from the [[American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers]] in 1989.<ref name=":2">{{cite web|title=21st Annual ASCAP Deems Taylor Award Recipients|url=https://www.ascap.com/en/eventsawards/awards/deems-taylor/feature/years/1988|publisher=The American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers|access-date=9 September 2017}}</ref>

For his popular and educational science writing, Hazen received the [[Elizabeth A. Wood|E.A. Wood]] Science Writing Award from the [[American Crystallographic Association]] in 1998,<ref>{{cite web|title=Past Award Winners|url=http://www.amercrystalassn.org/content/pages/main-past-award-winners|publisher=American Crystallographic Association|access-date=10 September 2017|archive-date=1 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201235051/http://www.amercrystalassn.org/content/pages/main-past-award-winners|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2012, the State Council of Higher Education for Virginia presented Hazen with its Outstanding Faculty Award.<ref>{{cite press release|title=Professor Hazen receives Virginia Outstanding Faculty Award|url=https://cos.gmu.edu/aoes/professor-hazen-receives-virginia-outstanding-faculty-award/|access-date=10 September 2017|work=Atmospheric, Oceanic, and Earth Sciences|publisher=George Mason University|date=30 January 2012}}</ref>

In 2014, Hazen was elected a Fellow of the [[Geochemical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fellows by Year |url=https://geochemsoc.org/honors/society-awards/geochemistry-fellows/fellows-by-year |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Geochemical Society |language=en}}</ref>

In 2015, Hazen was elected a Fellow of the [[Geological Society of America]].<ref>{{Cite journal |date=July 2015 |title=2015 GSA Fellows |url=https://rock.geosociety.org/gsatoday/archive/25/7/pdf/gt1507.pdf |journal=GSA Today: A Publication of the Geological Society of America |volume=25 |issue=7 |pages=16}}</ref> 

In 2019, Hazen was named a Fellow of the [[American Geophysical Union]].<ref>{{Cite journal |title=2019 Class of AGU Fellows Announced |url=https://eos.org/agu-news/2019-class-of-agu-fellows-announced |access-date=2020-06-19 |journal=Eos |year=2019 |language=en-US |doi=10.1029/2019eo131029 |last1=Bell |first1=Robin |last2=Holmes |first2=Mary |volume=100 |doi-access=free}}</ref> That year he was also elected a Foreign Member of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Иностранные члены РАН |url=https://www.ras.ru/members/personalstaff/foreignmembers.aspx?fmem=22 |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=www.ras.ru}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-08 |title=Hazen inducted into Russian Academy of Sciences |url=https://carnegiescience.edu/news/hazen-inducted-russian-academy-sciences |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=carnegiescience.edu |language=en}}</ref> 

In 2021, Hazen was awarded the Medal of Excellence in Mineralogical Sciences from the [[International Mineralogical Association]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Robert M. Hazen IMA Medal 2021|url=https://ima.univie.ac.at/|access-date=2021-06-11|website=IMA|language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2022, Hazen was granted an honorary doctorate of science by the [[American Museum of Natural History]]’s Richard Gilder Graduate School.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Commencement {{!}} Richard Gilder Graduate School |url=https://www.amnh.org/research/richard-gilder-graduate-school/school-overview/commencement |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=American Museum of Natural History |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-15 |title=City Life Org - The Museum's Richard Gilder Graduate School Confers PH.D. and MAT Degrees |url=https://thecitylife.org/2022/09/14/the-museums-richard-gilder-graduate-school-confers-ph-d-and-mat-degrees/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=City Life Org |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2025, Hazen was awarded the Marcus Milling Legendary Geoscientist Medal in by the [[American Geosciences Institute|American Geoscience Institute]], “in recognition of his lifetime of notable achievements in the geosciences and global impact across disciplines.”<ref>{{Cite web |last=Keane |first=Christopher |title=Dr. Robert Hazen Named 2025 Marcus Milling Legendary Geoscientist by AGI |url=https://www.americangeosciences.org/news/press-releases/2025-june-milling-medal/ |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=American Geosciences Institute |language=en}}</ref>  

Hazen has presented numerous [[named lecture]]s at universities. He gave a Directorate for Biological Sciences Distinguished Lecture at the [[National Science Foundation]] in 2007,<ref>{{cite news|title=The Emergence of Life on Earth...and Other Planets?|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=109624|access-date=10 September 2017|work=News|publisher=National Science Foundation|date=8 June 2007|language=en}}</ref> and was named the [[Sigma Xi]] Distinguished Lecturer for 2008–2010.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sigma Xi Distinguished Lecturers, 2008–2009|url=https://www.sigmaxi.org/programs/lectureships/past-lecturers/2008-2009|publisher=Sigma Xi|access-date=10 September 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Sigma Xi Distinguished Lecturers, 2009–2010|url=https://www.sigmaxi.org/programs/lectureships/past-lecturers/2009-2010|publisher=Sigma Xi|access-date=10 September 2017}}</ref> In 2011, Hazen gave the [[Uppsala University]] Linnaeus Lecture.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Celsius-Linnéföreläsning 2011 - Medfarms mediabibliotek |url=https://media.medfarm.uu.se/media921 |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=media.medfarm.uu.se}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-13 |title=Previous Lectures – Disciplinary Domain of Science and Technology – Uppsala University |url=https://www.uu.se/en/disciplinary-domain/science-and-technology/research/celsius-linnaeus-lectures/previous-lectures |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=www.uu.se |language=en}}</ref>  In 2025, he was chosen as the Hallimond Lecturer by the [[Mineralogical Society of Great Britain and Ireland]] and the Howard Flack Lecturer by the Swiss Crystallographic Society.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hallimond Lecture |url=https://www.minersoc.org/hallimond-lecture.html |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=Mineralogical Society of the UK and Ireland |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-10 |title=Howard Flack Crystallographic Lecture Series 2025 |url=https://scnat.ch/en/id/7ft49 |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=scnat.ch |language=en}}</ref>

Two fossil species, the Upper Miocene fossil dolphin, ''Cammackacetus hazenorum,'' and the Upper Miocene fossil hermit crab, ''Pagurus hazenorum,'' have been named in honor of Hazen and his wife Margaret.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://smithsonian.figshare.com/articles/book/_/23847438 |title=The Geology and Vertebrate Paleontology of Calvert Cliffs, Maryland, USA – Volume 2: Turtles and Toothed Whales |date=2023 |publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press |editor-last=Godfrey |editor-first=Stephen J. |series=Smithsonian Contributions to Paleobiology |volume=107 |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=142–147 |doi=10.5479/si.23847438}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wallaard |first1=Jonathan J.W. |last2=Fraaije |first2=René H.B. |last3=Van Bakel |first3=Barry W.M. |last4=Nance |first4=John R. |last5=Lindholm |first5=Adam |last6=Jagt |first6=John W.M. |date=2023-01-06 |title=New hermit crab species (Anomura, Paguroidea) from the upper Miocene St. Marys Formation of Maryland (USA), preserved in their host shells |url=https://www.mapress.com/zt/article/view/zootaxa.5227.3.7 |journal=Zootaxa |volume=5227 |issue=3 |pages=389–397 |doi=10.11646/zootaxa.5227.3.7 |pmid=37044682 |issn=1175-5334}}</ref>

Hazen is author of more than 400 articles and 20 books on science, history, and music.

== Family ==
Hazen's wife, Margee ''(née'' Margaret Joan Hindle), is a science writer and published historian.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Pinholster |first1=Ginger |title=Nominations Needed for Public Engagement Award |url=https://www.aaas.org/news/nominations-needed-public-engagement-award |access-date=30 August 2018 |work=AAAS|date=27 August 2010 |language=en}}</ref> Her late father, Howard Brooke Hindle, PhD (1918–2001), was a historian who studied the role of [[material culture]] in the history of the United States and served as Director of the [[National Museum of American History]] from 1974 to 1978.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Estrada |first1=Louie |title=Brooke Hindle, 82 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2001/06/06/brooke-hindle-82/2ea58a48-6b5d-4f5b-96ca-50171c8a3583/?noredirect=on |access-date=30 August 2018 |newspaper=Washington Post |date=6 June 2001}}</ref>  Hazen's late brother, Dan Chapin Hazen, PhD (1947–2015), was an academic research librarian who had been affiliated with the libraries at [[Harvard]], and was particularly recognized for his accomplishments to the [[Center for Research Libraries]] and advocacy of collections from Latin America.  Harvard has memorialized Dan Hazen by establishing two [[Financial endowment#Endowed professorships|chairs]] in his name.<ref>{{cite report |author=Center for Research Libraries |author-link=Center for Research Libraries |title=Transparency: Annual report fiscal year 2015: (July 1, 2014 – June 30, 2015) |url=https://www.crl.edu/sites/default/files/attachments/pages/CRL_AR2015.pdf }}</ref>
The Hazens have two children: Benjamin Hindle Hazen (born 1976) and Elizabeth Brooke Hazen (born 1978).<ref name=cv/>
